summary:
Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

What such a passport can contain is constrained. Legal gender change still requires a letter from a medical expert, and the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking between three and nine months. The self-identification bill was withdrawn in July 2025. Since the law passed in December 2013 took effect in 2014, changing gender on birth certificates and other official documents has no longer required surgery or sterilisation, which had been mandatory under the 1984 and 1985 laws.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics in employment, housing and public and private accommodations has been expressly prohibited since initiative Law 34.650, adopted by the Tweede Kamer on 3 July 2018 and the Eerste Kamer on 12 March 2019, published 25 September 2019 and in force 31 October 2019, which amended the Algemene wet gelijke behandeling to extend the ground of sex to those characteristics. Sexual orientation and disability were formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution in February 2023. A global LGBT rights index records bathroom access as protected in the Netherlands.

Discriminatory motive has been a statutory ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases since 1 July 2025, under a private-member's bill from Timmermans and Bikker, alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination, ECAD-P.

Official victimisation figures published by the Dutch government state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, comprising 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply under the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism. In 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people in 2025, up 7.5% on 2024 and 81% above the 2,654 recorded in 2022, according to figures released in April 2026 via Transgender Netwerk. Reports concerning transgender people rose 51% in a year, from 264 to 399. COC called the figures extremely worrying and noted that only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were secured in the year. These are raw report counts; the source provides no population denominator.

During the start of WorldPride Amsterdam in July 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants, and RITA warned that the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened its 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Halsema told the council that Amsterdam would tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride, backed by police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast. Recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

Detention carries a specific exposure. No law, regulation or official policy currently governs the placement of transgender detainees in the Netherlands; the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees. The Prison Service, DJI, confirmed to the Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights that placement rests on the gender designation in municipal records, the BRP, together with case-by-case factors including gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman held on a regular male wing on arrival before transfer to an Extra Care Facility; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis; a Limburg court sentencing ruling of 17 October 2017 (ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) on a trans woman facing placement in a men's prison; and a Hague appeals court ruling of 29 June 2020 (ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) on a trans man in a women's prison, both treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM wrote to the minister for legal protection, Weerwind, on 21 February 2024 asking for rules aligned with CPT standards placing detainees by gender identity; the detention institute DIZ said it was drafting guidelines that remain unpublished.
tangentialFactors:
The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026. A global LGBT rights comparison index rates it 2nd of 121 regions as a good place for LGBT people and records 52% support for LGBT openness, alongside homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change legal but requiring a medical diagnosis, non-binary recognised, discrimination illegal, employment and housing discrimination prohibited on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, and conversion therapy banned.

Public opinion measured on trans questions is favourable at national level. The 2023 Eurobarometer found 91% of Dutch people agreeing that transgender people should have the same rights as anyone else, and 84% agreeing that transgender persons should be able to change their civil documents to match their gender identity. A 2016 Netherlands Institute for Social Research report found 7% viewing homosexuality and bisexuality negatively and 10% viewing transgender people negatively.

Attitudes among young people moved the other way over the same period. The Utrecht University and Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys falling from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025.

Partner recognition is settled in law. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples began on 1 January 1998, same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 April 2001, marriages performed elsewhere in the state must be recognised under its constitutional charter, and since 2014 all marriage officiants have been prohibited from refusing services to same-sex couples.

Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, after the House passed the bill 127-23 in 2018 and the Senate 64-11 on 12 March 2019, following earlier cases in which the Dutch Institute for Human Rights treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender'. Transgender people are permitted to serve openly in the military.

Conversion practices targeting sexual orientation or gender identity are banned by a bill that passed the House in September 2025, the Senate on 16 June 2026 and was ratified on 8 September 2026; such therapies have been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012. Gender-affirming care for trans youth is publicly recommended: 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines endorsed by eight medical and patient organisations recommend puberty blockers at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, top surgery is available to patients over 16, and in July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate.

The 1985 to 2014 requirement of gender-affirming surgery and forced sterilisation was replaced by the law effective in 2014. The state issued a formal apology in December 2020 and implemented a €5,000 compensation scheme that month for an estimated 2,000 people sterilised under the prior law, following a February 2020 class-action lawsuit and a November 2021 cabinet announcement of eligibility.
localsOnly:
Changing legal gender remains an administrative process that requires a letter from a medical expert rather than self-declaration. The Transgender Act, a self-identification bill, was withdrawn in July 2025. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, with no general legislation, so each designation is court-decided: the District Court of Limburg granted 'sex cannot be determined' on 28 May 2018, Leonne Zeegers received a Dutch passport with an 'X' in October 2018 and Nanoah Struik in July 2019, a July 2021 district court allowed a gender X birth certificate for a self-identified non-binary individual, and a December 2021 ruling dropped psychologist certification for X in passports. Since 1993 a birth certificate may state 'sex cannot be determined' where a newborn's sex is unclear.

Placement in custody is decided without a governing rule. DJI confirmed that the gender designation in the BRP drives placement alongside case-by-case factors, and transgender detainees are frequently held on an Extra Care Facility wing to protect them from other detainees, in the company of people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. NJCM's criminal-law working group stated on 22 February 2024 that the absence of any law or regulation on the placement of transgender detainees is worrying and undesirable, noted the group's vulnerable position and international research documenting discrimination and sexual violence, and highlighted the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands. DIZ said it was drafting guidelines, which have not been published.

Employment, housing and public and private accommodation discrimination is prohibited on grounds covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics. A 'single fact' loophole that allowed religious schools to dismiss staff was closed by bills passed in 2014 and 2015, effective 1 July 2015. Compensation of €5,000 remains available to people sterilised under the 1985 law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; the statistics cited here rest on police recording practice through ECAD-P rather than on a statutory category, and the number of convictions recorded for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in 2025 is six.

Whether the aggravating-motive provision in force from 1 July 2025 applies to gender identity is unresolved in these sources. One index states that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only, which sits alongside the new penalty-enhancement mechanism; the sources do not reconcile the two.

The victimisation figures published by the Dutch government give no general-population comparator, so the 17% transgender and 22% intersex physical or sexual violence figures cannot be read against a background rate from these sources.

Report volumes are raw counts without denominators. The 4,800 reports in 2025, the trans-specific rise from 264 to 399, and the 25 to 45 reports per recent Pride are counts of reports, not rates, and the sources provide no basis for ranking the Netherlands against other jurisdictions on them. RITA itself states that the 70-plus WorldPride reports are only a fraction of the total, so the true incident volume for that period is not established.

No official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the guidelines DIZ said it was drafting remain unpublished.

Whether the July 2020 announcement that the Netherlands was considering abolishing gender markers on official identity documents from 2025 proceeded is not sourced here. Whether gender identity is among the grounds written into Article 1 of the Constitution in February 2023 is also not stated in these sources, which name sexual orientation and disability.
